DWL held the wine in its warehouse; HMRC traced the supply chain and concluded insufficient evidence that excise duty had been paid due to missing, de-registered, or hijacked companies in the chain.. HMRC issued a notice of assessment on 17 October 2013 for £3,729,381 for the period 21 February 2011 to 15 May 2012, on the basis that the goods were held outside a duty suspension arrangement and UK excise duty had not been paid.. The FTT framed three preliminary issues, the central one being whether a de facto or legal control holder who does not physically possess the goods can 'hold' the goods under Regulation 6(1)(b)/Article 7(2)(b).. The UT decision in B&M Retail Ltd v HMRC (2016) and the later Davison & Robinson Ltd v HMRC (2019) informed HMRC policy to assess the earliest possible holding outside a duty suspension when evidence could support more than one release for consumption.. The FTT’s holding issue was discussed as obiter in the UT decision, which remitted to the FTT for substantive determination with full facts.. The court references multiple EC and domestic authorities, including Perfect, WR, and Jacobson, to interpret 'holding' and the timing of duty points.
Case Summary: This Court of Appeal decision concerns the meaning of 'holding' under the EU excise regime and the UK transposing regulations, including whether control without physical possession suffices and whether there is a requirement to intend to assert that control. The case traces a multi-year tax-litigation path from HMRC’s assessment of excise duty on wine through FTT and UT decisions and engages doctrinal authorities like Perfect/WR. The final holding in this CA appeal is not stated in the provided text, but the appeal centers on the correct legal test for 'holding' and the appropriateness of preliminary determination.

Key Facts: Boak Building, 1-7 Station Street, Central Walsall, built ~1906; listed building status; later delisted after fire. Property owned by Mr Chinderpal Singh; Western Trading Limited holds/manages portions of the portfolio. Fire on 24 July 2012 destroyed the Boak Building; policy covered rebuilding (reinstatement) and rent loss costs. Sum insured for buildings: £2,121,800; market value before fire ~£75,000; pre-fire redevelopment plans for 31 flats. Memorandum to Section A reinstatement included: cost of rebuilding equals indemnity, with conditions (reasonable despatch, incurred costs, etc.). Judge Mackie QC (Mercantile Court) held Western Trading had indemnity rights up to policy limits for reinstatement cost and granted a declaration; insurers appealed. Issues included (i) whether Western Trading had insurable interest and was indemnified; (ii) whether declaration was appropriate where reinstatement might not occur; (iii) interpretation of reinstatement and its cost as the measure of indemnity. The Court of Appeal ultimately held that the reinstatement cost is the prima facie measure of indemnity under the Memorandum, that a declaration is a suitable remedy with appropriate wording, and that damages were not awarded; costs were adjusted
Case Summary: This appeal concerned whether a company insured under a policy covering fire damage to a building is entitled to an indemnity equal to the cost of reinstating the building, and whether a declaration granting such indemnity up to the policy limit is appropriate where reinstatement may or may not proceed. The High Court had granted a declaration, and the Court of Appeal held that reinstatement cost is the prima facie measure of indemnity under the Memorandum, that a properly drafted declaration can be an appropriate remedy, and that the form of wording must reflect insurable interest and non-avoidance of the policy. The court varied the declaration and affirmed that, if reinstatement occurs, the insurer must indemnify up to the policy limit; it declined damages in lieu of the declaration and adjusted the costs order accordingly.

Reasoning: The Court of Appeal held that, on the facts, the claim accrued on 12 October 2007 (distribution) and that section 21(1)(b) of the Limitation Act 1980 can apply where a trustee indirectly receives trust property via a company controlled by the trustee. While the judge below had granted summary judgment on limitation, the Court of Appeal found genuine issues of fact regarding whether interim accounts and any revaluation were properly prepared and relied on, and whether the distribution was lawful. The court stated that the appeal should focus on whether the distribution in specie was lawful, with factual investigations required. It also recognized that section 32 postponement is a potential path, but declined to determine it at summary judgment, given there were disputed facts (e.g., directors’ knowledge and the existence of interim accounts). The decision relied on authorities interpreting section 21(1)(b) including Pantone, Miller v Bain, and subsequent treatment of indirect receipt through entities under control of trustees, as well as principles from Cave and Jetivia regarding discovery and deliberate concealment.”

Key Facts: Brooks challenged an 11-day detention following the expiry of the custodial element of an extended sentence under the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (CJA 2003).. Under CJA 2003 s247(2), the State has a duty to release upon serving half the custodial term, with licence continuing post-release; Brooks’ release would have been 23 April 2012 but occurred on 4 May 2012 due to a 14-day disciplinary detention award.. The 14 days were imposed after an offense against discipline on 2 February 2012 and a hearing on 1 March 2012 before an Independent Adjudicator (IA).. The District Judge presiding on 1 March 2012 refused recusal; Brooks received an additional 14 days detention under rule 60A(1).. A consent order (sealed 18 May 2012) quashed the findings of guilt and the award of additional days; Brooks remained in detention for 11 days before the quashing order was enacted.. Laing J (Oct 2014) held the detention unlawful under Article 5 and awarded damages (£1,000); the Secretary of State appealed.. The Court of Appeal held that detention was not unlawful and allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal, effectively reversing the Laing J decision on the Article 5 issue.. The case discusses whether a quashing order should be treated as retroactively voiding an administrative act and the implications for detention already performed.
Case Summary: This appeal concerns whether the detention of Matthew Brooks for 11 days beyond the expiry of the custodial term, following an alleged disciplinary offence and an award of additional days, was lawful. The High Court held that the detention breached Article 5 and awarded damages. The Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal, holding that detention remained lawful under the statutory regime and that the quashing of the adjudicator’s findings did not render the detention unlawfully imposed. The decision engages questions of statutory interpretation, the status of disciplinary awards as judicial acts, and the reach of ECHR protections in the context of administrative detention.

Abstract: Court of Appeal decision addressing the tax treatment of foreign tax credits (DTR) in a rate-boosting scheme designed to maximise Case V foreign tax credits through an intragroup dividend chain. The appeal largely fails, with the court accepting HMRC’s positions on several points but allowing relief for a narrow amount (£811,800) arising from a specific dividend event. The judgment provides a detailed statutory interpretation of ICTA 1988 provisions governing underlying tax, the mixer cap, higher-level dividends and related concepts, and clarifies the relationship between actual, paid, and deemed taxes in the unilateral relief regime.

Key Facts: Site located in the Tyne Riverside Enterprise Zone (Feb 1996–18 Feb 2006).. Golden Contract (17 Feb 2006) modified the standard JCT contract with Contractor’s Design, creating multiple Works Options.. DC1 built under Change Order 1 (Nov 2009) following Variation Agreements One and Two; DC2 and DC3 were contemplated by later Change Orders 2 (April 2011) and 3 (April 2011).. Expenditures on DC2 and DC3 were formalised in SDAs (4–5 Apr 2011) as distinct from the Golden Contract.. Upper Tribunal decisions [2019] UKUT 342 (TCC) and [2020] UKUT 356 (TCC) addressed EZAs and apportionment; HMRC appealed; the LLPs cross‑appealed.. The CA held Change Orders 2 and 3 were not issued under clause 12 of the Golden Contract and did not create a new, compliant variation of the Golden Contract; instead, DC2/DC3 were governed by separate contracts (SDAs).. EZAs depend on the expenditure being within the statutory time limits (10 years post site inclusion, or 20 years if incurred under a contract entered within the 10-year window). The 2011 SDAs fall outside the initial 10-year window, and the court’s analysis treated DC2/DC3 as new contracts rather than variances.
Case Summary: This Court of Appeal decision revisits the interplay between tax relief for enterprise zone expenditure and contract law, specifically whether post‑award changes to a bespoke build contract amount to a variation or a rescission, and whether expenditures on the later DC2/DC3 data centres qualify for EZAs under the time limits in the CAA 2001. The court parses the structure of the Golden Contract, the sequence of Change Orders and Variation Agreements, and the separate SDAs, concluding that the later works were not incurred under the same contract within the statutory time frame and thus EZAs are not available for those expenditures. The ruling tightens the criteria for treating subsequent construction as qualifying expenditure for EZAs when driven by altered contractual arrangements after an initial contract has been exhausted.

How do authorities such as Castellain v Preston, Reynolds v Phoenix, Leppard v Excess Insurance, and Lonsdale v Black Arrow Group guide the measure of indemnity?. What is the timing/condition for payment under the Memorandum (costs must be incurred; reinstatement must be commenced with reasonable despatch)?. Can a declaration be amended to cure drafting defects without altering substantive rights granted by the original declaration?

{"content": "Legal Analysis:
Legal Issues: Whether English exclusive jurisdiction applies to excess policies with PPJC and/or clause 11. Effect of PPJC on exclusive jurisdiction in absence of a primary policy clause. Relation between clause 11 (Global Umbrella) and clause 12 (First/Third Excess) in determining jurisdiction. Whether Scotland-origin policy exception affects interpretation of jurisdiction clauses. Appropriate standard of proof for breach of an arbitration/exclusive jurisdiction clause (high degree of probability). Role of comity and delay considerations (Ecobank v Tanoh) in exclusive jurisdiction cases. Impact of English law/jurisdiction mandatory language on interpretation of the clauses. Policy-anchored forum selection in multi-layer insurance arrangements
Reasoning: The court adopted a principled construction of the relevant policy clauses. It held that clause 11 of the Global Umbrella Policy is intended to provide the same law and same jurisdiction as the primary policy. Because the Global CGL did not contain a jurisdiction clause, clause 11 effectively imports English jurisdiction and English law as mandatory for disputes under the umbrella policy. For the First and Third Excess Policies, clause 12 explicitly provides exclusive English jurisdiction, and there was no need to rely on PPJC to read them in. The PPJC is designed to operate with primary policies containing express law/jurisdiction clauses; applying it to a policy lacking such clause would create a floating law/jurisdiction framework, which the court rejected. The judge’s test for breach of an exclusive jurisdiction clause requires a negative right not to be sued, proven to a high degree of probability; this standard is robustly supported by authorities (e.g., Emmott; Ecobank v Tanoh). The court rejected arguments that the Scottish exceptions or non-exclusive readings should apply, and it reaffirmed that English law and English jurisdiction are typically interpreted as mandatory in these contexts. The analysis drew on a broad line of authorities to support the interpretation that there is an intended single governing forum and law for disputes under the insurance tower, which in this case is the English Commercial Court. The decision relies on commercial certainty and the reasonable expectations of businesses in cross-border insurance arrangements, and it adheres to long-standing authority that an English-law-and-English-forum clause should be construed as exclusive where the language is imperative and the commercial purpose is clear.

Key Facts: Claimants/insurers challenge the 1997 Act and regulations as infringing A1P1 rights through CRU recoveries in long-tail disease claims. CRU certificates require repayment of recoverable benefits awarded in compensation claims. Judgment at first instance (Henshaw J) found unlawful readings down of the 1997 Act in three scenarios (contributory negligence, divisible disease, missing contributors) and in a third time period (indivisible disease with missing contributors) and in a fourth scenario the reading down was not found. Cross-appeals concern a potential fourth scenario (CRU certificates not matching a head of loss) and recognition of a fifth scenario (compromised CRU certificates). Damages claims potentially to be transferred to the Chancery Division for case management. Hearing dates for the Court of Appeal: 12–14 October 2021; judgment delivered 14 January 2022. Neutral citations and case captions reflect appeals from the Administrative Court in the Queen’s Bench Division; the substantive issues center on compatibility with A1P1 and proportionality
Case Summary: The Court of Appeal considers whether the 1997 Act and its regulations infringe article 1 of the first protocol (A1P1) of the European Convention on Human Rights. Aviva and Swiss Re challenge obligations to repay recoverable benefits via CRU certificates in long-tail disease cases. The court applies Bank Mellat’s four-stage test, upholds infringement findings in three scenarios, finds no infringement in a fourth, and remits damages-related issues to the Chancery Division for further determination. Cross-appeals concerning remaining scenarios are addressed, with the fifth scenario acknowledged as not giving rise to a remedy.

Parties: SWA DEVELOPMENTS LTD v BURKE
Key Facts: Lease granted in 2006 to Mr Patrick Burke requiring extensive repair; bulk of repairs not completed. Dilapidations reappeared in a 3 March 2010 schedule connected to a proposed assignment to Barrington Burke. Freehold purchased by the Claimant on 31 July 2013 with dilapidations still outstanding. Pub refurbishment in December 2013; Vincent Power took over management. Lease covenants included prohibition on parting with or sharing possession and an obligation for the tenant to be actively involved in managing the business. Judge found Burke had abandoned possession to Barrington Burke, and that this amounted to a waiver in part; but Power’s involvement was not covered by the section 146 notice and did not amount to a waiver of that breach. Renewed application for relief from forfeiture; the judge cited Magnic v Ul-Hassan on the starting point for discretion and the policy that relief is not an implied penalty. Judge treated the extremely unusual background of the case as a decisive factor against granting relief. Court of Appeal refused permission to appeal, endorsing the first instance approach and the weighting given to landlord conduct and tenant disengagement
Case Summary: This appeal concerns whether the landlord’s right of re-entry for unpaid rent or breach of covenant should be exercised as a forfeiture sanction or whether relief from forfeiture should be granted. The County Court found breaches arising from disrepair and from the tenant’s disengagement; the tenant sought relief from forfeiture. The Court of Appeal held there was no error in principle in the judge’s exercise of discretion and refused permission to appeal, particularly given the extraordinary factual background and the weight given to the landlord’s conduct versus the tenant’s lack of involvement.

Issue 3: Whether the other requirements of s61(4) are satisfied so as to deem the satellites to belong to IMSO as at 15 April 1999, including (a) the ‘requirement’ of the Leases to provide the satellites; (b) the chronological flow of s61(4) in light of launch costs; (c) whether the tailpiece of s61(4) applies and its consequences.
Reasoning: The Court of Appeal reinforces that section 78(1) functions as a valuation deeming provision rather than an ownership-transfer mechanism. The court also scrutinises the connection between expenditure on launch costs and the provision of plant. It finds that expenditure on launch costs cannot be described as expenditure on the provision of the satellites themselves, and, for I-2, the existence of a lease obligation does not convert launch costs into capital expenditure on plant under section 61(4). The decision distinguishes I-2 versus I-3 structures and rejects arguments that a general obligation to comply with laws translates into a specific obligation to incur launch expenditures under s61(4). The judgment aligns with the approach that deems should not create unintended disposals or ownership transfers without explicit statutory direction and highlights the valuation nature of s78 as a mechanism rather than a transfer of title.

Reasoning: The Court analyzed the pleadings and the documents submitted to determine what issues were fairly and squarely raised during the FTT and UT processes. It concluded that Ground 2—centering on the application of section 11 and the reacquisition of assets as qualifying expenditure—was not explicitly pleaded as a Ground 2 in the HMRC or Taxpayer submissions and was not clearly advanced as a live issue in the pleadings. The Court underscored the necessity for precise articulation of grounds of appeal in the permission process and concluded that Ground 2 arose only in response to UT commentary, not as a pleaded issue before the tribunals. Therefore, while the UT’s reversal on Issue 1 (the Ramsay-based disposal) remained intact as a matter of fact, the Court avoided deciding Ground 2 on its merits by treating it as improperly raised. The decision reflects tight adherence to procedural compliance for new grounds and clarifies the scope of appellate review in tax cases where ground-shifting occurred during proceedings. The court acknowledged the authorities cited by both sides (Ramsay, Tower, BMBF, Ensign) but found no adequate articulation in the pleadings to make Ground 2 live before the FTT or UT, rendering it a new appeal point rather than an existing issue. The overall stance preserves the UT’s outcome on Issue 1 but limits the procedural reach of a late-appeal Ground 2, leaving the substantive merits on that ground unresolved.

Effect of 'premises test' vs 'plant-function' on capital allowances. Role of prior authorities in determining whether assets are plant or premises
Reasoning: The Court of Appeal reaffirmed that there is no statutory definition of 'plant' and that determining whether something is 'plant' is a question of fact or fact and degree. It endorsed the long-standing distinction between 'premises' (setting) and 'plant' (the means of carrying on business in an appropriately prepared setting). The decision emphasised that mere possession of plant-like functions or being purpose-built does not automatically transform premises into plant. Dilapidations reappeared in a 3 March 2010 schedule connected to a proposed assignment to Barrington Burke. Freehold purchased by the Claimant on 31 July 2013 with dilapidations still outstanding. Pub refurbishment in December 2013; Vincent Power took over management. Lease covenants included prohibition on parting with or sharing possession and an obligation for the tenant to be actively involved in managing the business. Judge found Burke had abandoned possession to Barrington Burke, and that this amounted to a waiver in part; but Power’s involvement was not covered by the section 146 notice and did not amount to a waiver of that breach. Renewed application for relief from forfeiture; the judge cited Magnic v Ul-Hassan on the starting point for discretion and the policy that relief is not an implied penalty. Judge treated the extremely unusual background of the case as a decisive factor against granting relief. Court of Appeal refused permission to appeal, endorsing the first instance approach and the weighting given to landlord conduct and tenant disengagement
Case Summary: This appeal concerns whether the landlord’s right of re-entry for unpaid rent or breach of covenant should be exercised as a forfeiture sanction or whether relief from forfeiture should be granted. The County Court found breaches arising from disrepair and from the tenant’s disengagement; the tenant sought relief from forfeiture. The Court of Appeal held there was no error in principle in the judge’s exercise of discretion and refused permission to appeal, particularly given the extraordinary factual background and the weight given to the landlord’s conduct versus the tenant’s lack of involvement.

Whether the proper approach is objective foreseeability (information reasonably available) or subjective foresight. Whether the concept of 'assumption of responsibility' is a necessary or overarching test for duty of care in this case. Whether the case should follow Caparo's tripartite framework or incremental development per Robinson. Whether the court could or should draw analogies from the 'audit duty' in Rihan v Ernst & Young. Whether the alleged 'red flags' and Burkey memorandum evidence established the bank's knowledge and duty to act. Limitation: whether the alleged negligence occurred before the arrestee's conviction and whether damages outside the limitation period should be considered. Nature and scope of the contractual indemnity (paras. 19.1 and 19.2) and how it interacts with the tort claim (pleaded indemnities)
Reasoning: The court emphasizes an objective standard of foreseeability based on information reasonably available to the bank at the relevant time, rejecting claims that relied on subjective perception of risk. It rejects the notion that 'assumption of responsibility' is a universal foundation for a duty of care in this economic-loss scenario. The decision relies on an incremental, Robinson-style approach to novel negligence cases, with Caparo factors used as guidance rather than a rigid test. The panel holds that having chosen not to anticipate the specific Romanian risk, the bank could not be liable for losses arising from the claimant's conviction. The court also examines the Burkey memorandum and the 'red flags' but concludes that the trial judge's findings about knowledge and escalation were open on the evidence. The possibility of relying on Rihan's 'audit duty' analogy is rejected as inapplicable to the conduct here. The limitation analysis follows established authorities (Khan v Falvey) and confirms the tort claim cannot be salvaged by reframing the duty as broader than the pleaded scope.

Dilapidations reappeared in a 3 March 2010 schedule connected to a proposed assignment to Barrington Burke. Freehold purchased by the Claimant on 31 July 2013 with dilapidations still outstanding. Pub refurbishment in December 2013; Vincent Power took over management. Lease covenants included prohibition on parting with or sharing possession and an obligation for the tenant to be actively involved in managing the business. Judge found Burke had abandoned possession to Barrington Burke, and that this amounted to a waiver in part; but Power’s involvement was not covered by the section 146 notice and did not amount to a waiver of that breach. Renewed application for relief from forfeiture; the judge cited Magnic v Ul-Hassan on the starting point for discretion and the policy that relief is not an implied penalty. Judge treated the extremely unusual background of the case as a decisive factor against granting relief. Court of Appeal refused permission to appeal, endorsing the first instance approach and the weighting given to landlord conduct and tenant disengagement
Case Summary: This appeal concerns whether the landlord’s right of re-entry for unpaid rent or breach of covenant should be exercised as a forfeiture sanction or whether relief from forfeiture should be granted. The County Court found breaches arising from disrepair and from the tenant’s disengagement; the tenant sought relief from forfeiture. The Court of Appeal held there was no error in principle in the judge’s exercise of discretion and refused permission to appeal, particularly given the extraordinary factual background and the weight given to the landlord’s conduct versus the tenant’s lack of involvement.

The High Court had previously quashed the inspector’s decision, but the Court of Appeal ultimately dismissed Broadview’s appeal. The court acknowledged a breach of one Planning Propriety Guidance provision (the tea-room/private representations) but found no material breach of natural justice or bias that would justify quashing the decision. The committee's decision was influenced by prior support from a Conservation Advisory Group (CAG) comprised of members also serving on the planning committee, leading to allegations of bias.. Persistent objections from local healthcare authorities regarding the need and potential impact of the proposed nursing home were inadequately addressed in the committee's discussions.
Case Summary: Costas Georgiou, acting for a local business association, challenged decisions made by the London Borough of Enfield to grant planning permission for a mental health nursing home within a Grade II listed building. The planning committee's decision, made by a narrow vote, raised concerns about the sufficiency of information and the appearance of bias due to overlapping memberships between the committee and the conservation advisory group. The High Court found that the council’s decisions lacked adequate consideration of material concerns, leading to their quashing based on the principles established in the case law surrounding bias and proper council conduct in planning decisions.

Legal Issues: Whether the planning inspector complied with procedural fairness rules in identifying and handling the main highway safety issues. Whether a Grampian condition could have been used to resolve highway safety concerns before development commenced. Impact of statements of common ground on identifying the main issues and the inspector’s discretion under Rule 16 to identify issues. Effect of third‑party representations on issue identification and fairness in an inquiry. Appropriateness of relying on Stage 1 Road Safety Audit and designer responses without independent speed checks. Whether the inspector’s post‑inquiry access to contemporaneous notes affected the fairness of the process. Role of Rule 7 and Rule 16 in informing participants and maintaining focus of inquiry without excluding relevant issues. Judicial approach to procedural fairness in planning inquiries, as supplemented by Hopkins Developments and other authorities
Reasoning: The Court of Appeal held that the inspector’s course of inquiry did not meet the standards of procedural fairness required in planning inquiries, particularly because the main highway safety issue (the pedestrian crossing) was highlighted by local residents and discussed at the inquiry, yet the inspector’s handling of the issue coupled with the pre‑inquiry and post‑inquiry materials did not adequately allow parties to respond to concerns raised by third parties. The court emphasized Hopkins Developments’ guidance that a party is entitled to know the opposing case and to respond to it, and that significant issues raised by third parties should be addressed. It accepted that a statement of common ground between the developer and the relevant authorities (Council and highway authority) did not bind the inspector to ignore issues raised by third parties; indeed, the inspector’s own questions to witnesses and the invocation of residents’ concerns during the inquiry meant fairness required giving the residents a meaningful opportunity to respond. Regarding the Grampian condition ground, the judge treated it as part of the fairness challenge; the Court noted that the inspector acknowledged the potential for a more suitable crossing point but gave little weight to the SoCGH’s unsupported assertion that a Grampian approach might be appropriate. Consequently, the inspector’s reasoning and the decision to proceed without addressing the Grampian option were not sufficiently explained, contributing to the quashing. The court reaffirmed that even if the main parties have agreed certain aspects in SoCGs, fairness requires attention to issues raised by the public, and that the inspector should provide opportunities to address those issues, particularly where safety concerns are highlighted. The decision also clarifies the role of post‑inquiry notes and contemporaneous material in assessing the fairness of the process, and it rejects the notion that an inquiry’s focus on a narrow set of issues precludes considering wider safety concerns raised by residents. The court’s approach aligns with Hopkins and related authorities and underscores that procedural fairness is a fact‑specific inquiry requiring careful attention to the sequence of documents, representations, and the inspector’s inquiry conduct.

Whether the development was correctly treated as a single project for the purposes of the EIA Regulations 2017, given that the bridge’s purpose was tied to future development.
Reasoning: The Court of Appeal concluded that the OR misinterpreted the nature of the benefits and fails to separate the benefits of granting consent for the bridge itself from benefits arising from potential future development. • Court of Appeal level provides strong persuasive authority for public authorities in JR challenges to procurement/franchise specifications.

Reasoning: The court reiterated the statutory framework of s149, including its duties to eliminate discrimination, advance equality of opportunity, and foster good relations. It accepted that the duty does not require a substantive outcome and does not prescribe a particular procedural moment for equality impact assessment. It endorsed that a decision-maker must have a proper understanding of apparent equality impacts before adopting a policy, citing authorities like Baker, Brown, Bailey, and Bracking. Importantly, the court acknowledged the possibility of a rolling equality assessment in exceptional circumstances where urgency and public transport disruption (due to COVID-19) justify accelerating the process, so long as the duty is nevertheless performed and there is an intention to continue scrutiny. The court also emphasized that, where material is not yet available, there is a duty to obtain it and to engage appropriate groups. The unusual factual features (urgent pandemic context, constrained transport, and the need to support walking and cycling) supported the rolling approach in this case, but not as a universal rule. The decision confirms that the duty was performed at the October 2020 report stage, with the understanding that detailed future equality assessments would follow in later stages. The court cautioned that this approach will not always be appropriate and that the degree of regard must be determined case-by-case.

Parties: Sustainable Totnes Action Group v Sarah Jane Williams v Devon County Council
Key Facts: Totnes, Devon, with narrow Elizabethan-era Fore Street and High Street leading to traffic congestion.. Devon County Council introduced an experimental traffic order (ETO) in 2013 to implement option two (circuitous routing) and later made it permanent as a TRO in 2014, effective 27 August 2014.. Bob the Bus (BTB) operates public service vehicles; the TRO affected its ability to serve Fore Street efficiently, leading to objections from BTB.. A public inquiry was argued to be required under regulation 9 of the 1996 Regulations due to alleged restrictions on public service vehicles.. Sustainable Totnes Action Group, later substituted by Ms. Sarah Jane Williams as claimant, challenged the TRO.. The Administrative Court quashed the TRO on regulation 9 grounds and obiter on section 122 grounds; the Court of Appeal upheld the judge's interpretation of 'restrict' and dismissed the appeal.. The decision focused on whether 'restrict' should be interpreted in a physical-restriction sense or to include broader effects (e.g., circuitous routing) on public service vehicles.
Case Summary: This Court of Appeal decision addresses whether a TRO and its experimental predecessor, implemented in Totnes to mitigate traffic congestion, restricted the passage of public service vehicles such that a public inquiry was required under Regulation 9(3)(b) of the 1996 Regulations. The court upheld the lower court’s view that the alterations produced a substantial practical restriction on public service vehicles and that the regulation required a public inquiry. It also noted obiter that the defendant’s obligation under s.122 of the 1984 Act to consider relevant factors had not been complied with, but did not decide that issue. The defendant’s appeal was dismissed, and the TRO remained in force.

Key Facts: Tower Bridge GP Limited acted as the representative member of the CFG VAT Group in a series of carbon credit transactions with Stratex Alliance Limited and related Cantor Fitzgerald entities.. Between 18 May 2009 and 3 June 2009, CFE purchased carbon credits in 17 transactions that were invoiced by Stratex, a taxable person, but Stratex was not VAT-registered and the invoices lacked a VRN and other required details.. Stratex invoices totalled £5,605,119.74 in VAT; CFE paid this amount and Tower Bridge sought to deduct the input tax in its period 06/09 VAT return.. Stratex’s address and VRN were not provided; Stratex could not be traced; HMRC inspectors found Stratex’s address through a corporate service provider and no corrective documentation was ever supplied.. HMRC denied the deduction in 2012 on the basis that the invoices were invalid and Stratex was not VAT-registered; this denial was upheld through successive reviews/appeals at the FTT and UT.. The central legal question is whether the right to deduct can be exercised where the taxpayer does not hold a valid VAT invoice, and whether corrected invoices can have retroactive effect to support a deduction.. The judgment discusses the distinctions between substantive conditions (e.g., the supplier being a taxable person, the transaction being a valid taxable supply) and formal conditions (e.g., the content of invoices as required by Article 226, and the process for correcting invoices).. The decision cites EU case law on the balance between fiscal neutrality and formal invoicing requirements, including the limits of national formalities beyond what the VAT Directive requires, and the potential retroactive effect of corrected invoices under EU law.
Case Summary: This appeal concerns whether Tower Bridge GP Limited could deduct input VAT on Stratex invoices that were not valid VAT invoices. The UT had denied the deduction, and the Court of Appeal examines whether correction of invoices and the possession of compliant invoicing details can retroactively permit the deduction, in light of EU VAT principles and post-Brexit retained EU law. The decision engages complex questions about substantive vs formal conditions for the right to deduct and the role of invoice contents in enabling checks by tax authorities.

The central legal question is whether the right to deduct can be exercised where the taxpayer does not hold a valid VAT invoice, and whether corrected invoices can have retroactive effect to support a deduction.. The judgment discusses the distinctions between substantive conditions (e.g., the supplier being a taxable person, the transaction being a valid taxable supply) and formal conditions (e.g., the content of invoices as required by Article 226, and the process for correcting invoices).. Case Summary: This appeal concerns whether Tower Bridge GP Limited could deduct input VAT on Stratex invoices that were not valid VAT invoices. The UT had denied the deduction, and the Court of Appeal examines whether correction of invoices and the possession of compliant invoicing details can retroactively permit the deduction, in light of EU VAT principles and post-Brexit retained EU law. The decision engages complex questions about substantive vs formal conditions for the right to deduct and the role of invoice contents in enabling checks by tax authorities.

The First Tier Tribunal found abuse; the Upper Tribunal reversed and held the scheme abusive; the Court of Appeal dismissed the university’s appeal. Legal issue: whether the EU principle of abuse of rights invalidates the VAT-saving scheme and, if so, the consequences. Outcome: appeal dismissed; the scheme was found to constitute abuse of rights; the VAT advantage was not permissible. Stratex’s address and VRN were not provided; Stratex could not be traced; HMRC inspectors found Stratex’s address through a corporate service provider and no corrective documentation was ever supplied.. HMRC denied the deduction in 2012 on the basis that the invoices were invalid and Stratex was not VAT-registered; this denial was upheld through successive reviews/appeals at the FTT and UT.. The central legal question is whether the right to deduct can be exercised where the taxpayer does not hold a valid VAT invoice, and whether corrected invoices can have retroactive effect to support a deduction.. The judgment discusses the distinctions between substantive conditions (e.g., the supplier being a taxable person, the transaction being a valid taxable supply) and formal conditions (e.g., the content of invoices as required by Article 226, and the process for correcting invoices).. The decision cites EU case law on the balance between fiscal neutrality and formal invoicing requirements, including the limits of national formalities beyond what the VAT Directive requires, and the potential retroactive effect of corrected invoices under EU law.
Case Summary: This appeal concerns whether Tower Bridge GP Limited could deduct input VAT on Stratex invoices that were not valid VAT invoices. The UT had denied the deduction, and the Court of Appeal examines whether correction of invoices and the possession of compliant invoicing details can retroactively permit the deduction, in light of EU VAT principles and post-Brexit retained EU law. Parties: The University of Huddersfield Higher Education Corporation v HM Revenue and Customs
Key Facts: University exempt supplies from VAT plus taxable elements and a low partial exemption recovery rate. 2 Grade II listed mills (East Mill and West Mill) refurbished via a structured scheme. Discretionary trust created to enable VAT planning; trust controlled by the University. Lease from University to Trust (20 years), and underlease from Trust back to University. Properties Ltd (unrelated to VAT group) engaged for refurbishment; invoice paid by University. Interposed transactions aimed at achieving 100% input VAT recovery while charging output VAT. Built-in mechanism to collapse the leasehold structure to crystallise the VAT saving. FTT found abuse in 2002; UT reversed in 2014/2015; CA upheld the abuse finding
Case Summary: Facts: The University of Huddersfield created a discretionary trust and a lease/underlease structure linked to refurbishing East Mill to obtain a full deduction of input VAT; the scheme involved interposed entities and a built-in mechanism to collapse the structure to secure an absolute VAT saving. The First Tier Tribunal found abuse; the Upper Tribunal reversed and held the scheme abusive; the Court of Appeal dismissed the university’s appeal. Legal issue: whether the EU principle of abuse of rights invalidates the VAT-saving scheme and, if so, the consequences. Outcome: appeal dismissed; the scheme was found to constitute abuse of rights; the VAT advantage was not permissible. Reasoning centers on applying the two Halifax tests, evaluating the object, effect, and purpose of the transactions, and remaking the scheme by removing abusive elements rather than rewriting past history.

Reasoning: The Court of Appeal rejected Hammonds’ argument for an overarching master contract, distinguishing the case from authorities like Trentham and Mamidoil. It treated the November 2015 discussions as insufficient to create a master contract and found any implied variation or implied exclusivity by conduct to be unsupported because such an implied contract was not pleaded and the trial record did not demonstrate a binding agreement to that effect. The court emphasized a case-by-case approach, noting that evolving contracts may exist but must be proven on the facts; it rejected attempts to convert the relationship into an implied or evolving contractual framework after the fact. On notice periods, the court endorsed the trial judge’s three-month period, noting it balanced the parties’ interests and reflected the fact that Hammonds could respond with an alternative product within a short timeframe (as evidenced by Imaginaria) and that longer periods could impose undue burdens. The appeal and cross-appeal were dismissed following a careful consideration of the authorities cited (e.g., Notting Hill Finance, Spar Shipping, Carmichael, Alpha, Hamsard) and the factual context. The judgment also acknowledged the court’s discretion regarding new points on appeal and reaffirmed the principle that new points should not be entertained if they would have affected the trial’s conduct had they been raised earlier.

Abstract: Court of Appeal (Civil Division) considers the scope and application of state immunity under the State Immunity Act 1978, focusing on functional immunity for pre-abdication conduct attributed to a serving head of state and the ‘colour of authority’ test. The decision clarifies when state actors and their contractors may be treated as acting under colour of public authority in civil proceedings.

Reasoning: The Court of Appeal rejected the trial judge’s emphasis on the Six Countries as connecting factors. It held that when applying the 1995 Act, the court must identify factors connecting the tort to each competing jurisdiction and assess their significance. The trial judge identified two connecting factors with the Six Countries (location of injuries and presence of those causing them) but also recognized potentially reducing factors. The Court of Appeal found the UK factors — notably where the tortious conduct occurred (the CIA requests for information by UK services), the services’ official capacity under UK law, and the claimant’s reasonable expectations that UK law would govern conduct involving UK security bodies — to be substantial. On this basis, and given the statutory framework and Law Commission rationale, the court concluded that English law should apply. It emphasized that displacement under s12 requires a clear preponderance of factors pointing to the other country and that the general rule under s11 is heavily weighted; therefore it must be displaced only in clear cases. The decision cites and distinguishes precedent such as Roerig v Valiant Trawlers Ltd, R (Al-Jedda) v Secretary of State for Defence, VTB Capital v Nutritek, and Entick v Carrington, as well as the Law Commission’s reports on the 1995 Act and Dicey’s description of the expectations rationale. The court’s reasoning highlights that the conduct in question bears a strong connection to English law because UK authorities were involved and the alleged torts were committed in contexts linked to English sovereignty and governance. The Court of Appeal thus concluded the English law was substantially more appropriate for determining the tort issues, rather than the Six Countries’ laws.”,

Case Summary: This Court of Appeal (Civil Division) decision addresses the applicable law governing tort claims brought by a detainee, Abu Zubayda, against the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Home Office, and the Attorney General. The claimant alleges that UK security services were aware of, and assisted in, torture conducted by the CIA at secret “black sites” in six countries. The central issue is whether English law or the law of the six foreign jurisdictions should govern the tort claims, under the Private International Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1995. The court held that it is substantially more appropriate for English law to apply, emphasizing the factors linking the tort to England and Wales and the parties’ reasonable expectations, over the six-country nexus. The decision clarifies the application of the 1995 Act’s displacement test and reinforces the primacy of the general rule, subject to very clear displacement circumstances. The ruling has potential implications for cross-border torts involving state actors and international security operations and for how courts assess the locus of the tort and applicable law.)

Parties: Al-Saadoon & Ors v The Secretary of State for Defence v Rahmatullah & ANR v The Secretary of State for Defence & Anr
Key Facts: British military involvement in Iraq (2003–2009) gave rise to numerous civil claims alleging ill-treatment, detention and in some cases unlawful killing of Iraqi civilians by British soldiers. Two groups of claims: public law (investigative obligations) and private law (compensation). Disputes about the reach of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) to acts abroad, especially after the occupation. The case considers several test cases (PIL 6, PIL 82, PIL 129, PIL 176, PIL 11, PIL 168, etc.) and the Rahmatullah/Ali claims involving handover to US custody. The Court discusses three categories of extra-territorial jurisdiction under Article 1 ECHR (state agent authority and control; effective control over an area; espace juridique). The judge ultimately rejects a universal “Soering-type” investigative duty under Article 3 and a general investigative duty under Article 5, but recognises potential narrow Article 3 investigative duties in two PIL test cases involving alleged complicity or transfer to torture. Occupation period and post-occupation period analyses; test of authority and control over individuals as a basis for jurisdiction. Handover and detention cases involving Camp Bucca and Camp Cropper (US custody) are discussed as background to Rahmatullah/Ali arguments
Case Summary: This appeal consolidates two linked strands (Al-Saadoon v SOSD and Rahmatullah v SOSD) addressing whether the United Kingdom could be held to respect ECHR rights for acts outside its territory during and after the Iraq War. The court reaffirms the centrality of Article 1 ECHR jurisdiction as territorially grounded, recognises limited extra-territorial exceptions (principally state agent authority and control, including public powers and power exercised by state agents), and scrutinises the extent to which the UK bears investigative duties under Articles 2–5 (and UNCAT) for handover/detention scenarios. The Court of Appeal concludes there is no general Soering-type investigative duty under Article 3 for handover cases, nor a universal investigative duty under Article 5 for detention, though narrow circumstances may give rise to Article 3 investigative duties in two specific test cases. It also discusses UNCAT rights and their domestic enforceability under UK law.

Abstract: Court of Appeal (Civil Division) considers the scope and application of state immunity under the State Immunity Act 1978, focusing on functional immunity for pre-abdication conduct attributed to a serving head of state and the ‘colour of authority’ test. The decision clarifies when state actors and their contractors may be treated as acting under colour of public authority in civil proceedings.

Reasoning: The Court of Appeal rejected the trial judge’s emphasis on the Six Countries as connecting factors. It held that when applying the 1995 Act, the court must identify factors connecting the tort to each competing jurisdiction and assess their significance. The trial judge identified two connecting factors with the Six Countries (location of injuries and presence of those causing them) but also recognized potentially reducing factors. The Court of Appeal found the UK factors — notably where the tortious conduct occurred (the CIA requests for information by UK services), the services’ official capacity under UK law, and the claimant’s reasonable expectations that UK law would govern conduct involving UK security bodies — to be substantial. On this basis, and given the statutory framework and Law Commission rationale, the court concluded that English law should apply. It emphasized that displacement under s12 requires a clear preponderance of factors pointing to the other country and that the general rule under s11 is heavily weighted; therefore it must be displaced only in clear cases. The decision cites and distinguishes precedent such as Roerig v Valiant Trawlers Ltd, R (Al-Jedda) v Secretary of State for Defence, VTB Capital v Nutritek, and Entick v Carrington, as well as the Law Commission’s reports on the 1995 Act and Dicey’s description of the expectations rationale. The court’s reasoning highlights that the conduct in question bears a strong connection to English law because UK authorities were involved and the alleged torts were committed in contexts linked to English sovereignty and governance. The Court of Appeal thus concluded the English law was substantially more appropriate for determining the tort issues, rather than the Six Countries’ laws.”,

Case Summary: This Court of Appeal (Civil Division) decision addresses the applicable law governing tort claims brought by a detainee, Abu Zubayda, against the UK Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Home Office, and the Attorney General. The claimant alleges that UK security services were aware of, and assisted in, torture conducted by the CIA at secret “black sites” in six countries. The central issue is whether English law or the law of the six foreign jurisdictions should govern the tort claims, under the Private International Law (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1995. The court held that it is substantially more appropriate for English law to apply, emphasizing the factors linking the tort to England and Wales and the parties’ reasonable expectations, over the six-country nexus. The decision clarifies the application of the 1995 Act’s displacement test and reinforces the primacy of the general rule, subject to very clear displacement circumstances. The ruling has potential implications for cross-border torts involving state actors and international security operations and for how courts assess the locus of the tort and applicable law.)

Parties: Al-Saadoon & Ors v The Secretary of State for Defence v Rahmatullah & ANR v The Secretary of State for Defence & Anr
Key Facts: British military involvement in Iraq (2003–2009) gave rise to numerous civil claims alleging ill-treatment, detention and in some cases unlawful killing of Iraqi civilians by British soldiers. Two groups of claims: public law (investigative obligations) and private law (compensation). Disputes about the reach of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) to acts abroad, especially after the occupation. The case considers several test cases (PIL 6, PIL 82, PIL 129, PIL 176, PIL 11, PIL 168, etc.) and the Rahmatullah/Ali claims involving handover to US custody. The Court discusses three categories of extra-territorial jurisdiction under Article 1 ECHR (state agent authority and control; effective control over an area; espace juridique). The judge ultimately rejects a universal “Soering-type” investigative duty under Article 3 and a general investigative duty under Article 5, but recognises potential narrow Article 3 investigative duties in two PIL test cases involving alleged complicity or transfer to torture. Occupation period and post-occupation period analyses; test of authority and control over individuals as a basis for jurisdiction. Handover and detention cases involving Camp Bucca and Camp Cropper (US custody) are discussed as background to Rahmatullah/Ali arguments
Case Summary: This appeal consolidates two linked strands (Al-Saadoon v SOSD and Rahmatullah v SOSD) addressing whether the United Kingdom could be held to respect ECHR rights for acts outside its territory during and after the Iraq War. The court reaffirms the centrality of Article 1 ECHR jurisdiction as territorially grounded, recognises limited extra-territorial exceptions (principally state agent authority and control, including public powers and power exercised by state agents), and scrutinises the extent to which the UK bears investigative duties under Articles 2–5 (and UNCAT) for handover/detention scenarios. The Court of Appeal concludes there is no general Soering-type investigative duty under Article 3 for handover cases, nor a universal investigative duty under Article 5 for detention, though narrow circumstances may give rise to Article 3 investigative duties in two specific test cases. It also discusses UNCAT rights and their domestic enforceability under UK law.

Key Facts: Idenix held European Patent No. 1 523 489 for 2'-branched nucleosides treating Flaviviridae (e.g., HCV). Gilead alleged lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, insufficiency, and added matter against the patent. Judge Arnold (2014) found the patent invalid for lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, and insufficiency, rejecting added matter except in relation to claim 4. Idenix appealed arguing: priority entitlement of Pharmasset PCT; common general knowledge; invention plausibility; enablement across the breadth; and amendments to the claims. The case involved extensive discussion of common general knowledge, publications (Carroll et al., De Francesco & Rice, Walker & Hong), Savannah conference proceedings, and post-published evidence. The trial included 11 days of evidence and 4 days of hearing on appeal; the matter involved a large landscape of nucleoside analogues and the NS5B polymerase target in HCV. Issues included the priority chain (Route 1-3) for Pharmasset’s patent rights under US law; whether 2'-methyl-up-2'-hydroxy-down nucleosides were common general knowledge; and whether the claims were plausible across their broad scope
Case Summary: The Court of Appeal scrutinised the European patent owned by Idenix (EP 1,523,489) directed to 2'-branched nucleosides for Flaviviridae infections, notably HCV. It rejected Idenix’s arguments that Pharmasset-era publications and common general knowledge made the claimed invention plausible and that the patent contributed a technical advance across its broad claim scope. The court found insufficiency (not enabling the invention across the breadth without undue burden) and lack of plausible anti-Flaviviridae activity; it also held that the primary claim 1 as granted (and as proposed to be amended) lacked a plausible technical contribution. The decision leaves novelty largely unaddressed and raises important interim conclusions on priority transfer mechanisms under US law and on the admissibility of post-published evidence in assessing plausibility. The appeal was dismissed, with the lower court’s conclusions on insufficiency and lack of plausible utility upheld.

Legal Issues: patent_invalidity_insufficiency. plausibility_requirement. common_general_knowledge. obviousness. priority_rules. added_matter. novelty_not_decided. enablement
Reasoning: The court analysed whether substantial portions of the claimed compounds could be predicted to have anti-Flaviviridae activity as of June 2003. It held that there was no robust common general knowledge that 2'-methyl-up-2'-hydroxy-down nucleoside analogues would be efficacious against HCV, and that the patent’s breadth did not reflect a plausible technical contribution. The decision applied the plausibility standard from Human Genome Sciences v Lilly and Warner-Lambert v Generics, emphasizing that a technical effect must be plausible in light of the patent and common general knowledge. The court rejected Idenix’s reliance on Carroll, De Francesco & Rice, Walker & Hong, and Savannah conference materials as establishing common general knowledge by the priority date. It also scrutinised the patent’s enablement and found that the disclosure would require undue burden to synthesize and screen billions of compounds, given the 2'-methyl-up-2'-fluoro-down motif. The judges also discussed the challenges in retrosynthetic analysis and fluorination steps, finding that the patent gave insufficient guidance for skilled craftsmen to make the claimed compounds. On the priority issue, the court affirmed the need to determine whether Pharmasset Barbados could be a successor in title under 35 USC §261 and international Paris Convention rules, ultimately accepting the lower court’s approach that equitable title could be sufficient for priority in Route 2 or Route 3 scenarios. Overall, the decision underscores that broad, speculative claims without a credible technical contribution will fail for insufficiency and lack of plausibility, even if there may be a technical basis in the field. The Court affirmed that the patent did not provide a sufficiently plausible path to activity across its breadth, and it did not overturn the lower court’s insufficiency ruling on the core claims.

Parties: Sandoz Limited v Bristol-Myers Squibb Holdings Ireland Unlimited Company v Teva Pharmaceuticals Limited v TEVA UK Limited
Key Facts: The case centers on plausibility as a criterion for patent validity (EPC framework) in the context of a single compound claim for apixaban, a factor Xa inhibitor.. The patent in suit: European Patent (UK) No. 1 427 415 and its SPC based on the patent, expiring in 2026.. Closely related to prior art and plausibility doctrine developed in EPO Board of Appeal decisions and the Enlarged Board in G 2/21.. Application published as WO 03/026652; find that plausibility must be tested against the application, not extrapolated from the patent alone.. Closest pre-existing art identified as WO 131 (Du Pont/BMS) related to factor Xa inhibitors.. The judge’s analysis concluded that the alleged technical effect (potent factor Xa inhibition) was not plausibly demonstrated across substantially all claimed compounds within the disclosure at the filing date.. The decision addresses the admissibility and role of post-published evidence in both inventive step and sufficiency contexts, referencing G 2/21 and related UK/EPO jurisprudence.. Outcome: the patent and SPC were held invalid by the Court of Appeal; claimants Sandoz and Teva prevailed on appeal.
Case Summary: This appeal concerns the validity of European Patent (UK) No. 1 427 415 directed to a lactam-containing class of factor Xa inhibitors, notably apixaban. Sandoz and Teva challenged the patent on grounds including lack of plausibility that the compound would have factor Xa inhibitory activity. The High Court found the patent invalid; the Court of Appeal upheld, holding that plausibility must be demonstrated in the application as filed and that post-published data cannot salvage a lack of plausibility. The decision discusses EPO case law (G 2/21) and clarifies the approach to plausibility for a single compound claim and for second medical use-like questions, with implications for future patentability analyses.

Reasoning: The court reaffirmed the precept that constructive dismissal requires a repudiatory breach assessed by the cumulative conduct, not the mere perception of unreasonableness. Citing Western Excavating v Sharp, the tribunal must show that, taken as a whole, the employer’s conduct amounted to a breach of contract capable of terminating the contract without notice. The Tribunal’s findings—particularly that the alleged ‘last straw’ (22 March 2012) was not a continuing breach and that monitoring after that date was in line with policy—meant there was no repudiatory breach. The Court of Appeal noted that the tribunal did not need to repeatedly use the noun ‘constructive dismissal’ if its reasoning, in light of section 95(1)(c) ERA 1996 and related authorities (Meikle, Lewis, Woods), properly disposed of the case. The absence of an explicit concluding sentence in paragraph 62.12 was considered by the court to be implied by the comprehensive reasoning and findings; accordingly, the Tribunal’s conclusions were sound. The panel also emphasized that the protected-disclosure claim failed due to credibility findings and the absence of a genuine, good-faith disclosure that would meet statutory requirements.

Reasoning: The court applied the separability principle to distinguish a protected-disclosure context from conduct-based dismissal. It concluded that the tribunal correctly treated the protected disclosures as a separate context from the bank’s decision to dismiss. While Jhuti requires scrutiny of the decision-makers’ motivations, the court found insufficient evidence to attribute the dismissal motive to the protected disclosures through the decision-makers’ mindset. It emphasized the need to identify the genuine principal reason for dismissal and rejected arguments that the protected disclosures, even if contemporaneous with the challenged conduct, automatically negate a conduct-based reason. The judgment relied on Fecitt for the standard that protected disclosures must materially influence the detriment, and on Jhuti/Page/Martin-type jurisprudence to guard against attributing motive without clear, separable evidence. The panel also recognized the risk of over-extending whistleblowing protections in cases where the conduct itself provides a legitimate, separable basis for dismissal.

Reasoning: Lord Justice Kitchin held that s41 is a procedural mechanism enabling registration of a series of trade marks, not a new form of 'series mark'. The words of s41(2) contemplate a bundle of marks that resemble each other in material particulars and differ only in non-distinctive aspects. The Registrar may register a series under one reference number, and if accepted, all marks in the series are protected as separate marks, but the series remains a bundle, not a single sign. The court found the Comptroller’s interpretation consistent with the ordinary meaning of the statute and compatible with EU law, citing Sieckmann, Libertel, Heidelberger, and IP Translator to emphasise graphical representation requirements and the need for certainty in the register. The decision rejects Fox’s argument that the series format misleads or conflicts with EU law, and declines to refer questions to the ECJ. The court treated the series as a registration of multiple marks under a single registration, with the same protection framework as individual marks, subject to s41’s conditions. The outcome preserves the infringement finding against Fox and upholds the use of a series registration under the 1994 Act, while not finding any invalidity of CEL’s marks solely on compatibility grounds.

The Court found no formal profit-sharing agreement beyond equal dividends from FCM London; the Defendants’ entitlement to profits was limited to dividends, not per-transaction profit sharing.
Case Summary: This appeal concerns a US$2.2 million termination fee payable under a loan facility to an offshore fund and the subsequent diversion of US$1.1 million (and related amounts) to a related corporate vehicle and individuals. The High Court held the defendants liable for breach of fiduciary duties, dishonest assistance, and conspiracy, with the Fund asserting an equitable proprietary claim to the diverted sums. Reasoning: The judges rejected the FCA’s submission that 'knowledge' extends to the knowledge of all disapplications or exemptions, arguing that such an approach would cast a much wider net and diverge from the legislature’s use of 'knowingly' in the context of section 21(1). They stressed that Section 21(2) does not create additional elements of the contravention; if the primary contravention is proven (i.e., the elements in s21(1) are satisfied), knowledge can be limited to awareness of those facts. The panel highlighted the practical effect: the court should not be required to examine every exemption or disapplication in depth; the regulator’s findings of knowledge would typically focus on the facts that establish the contravention. It was countered that a broader approach could lead to an excessively wide liability; but the Court held that such an outcome is not what the legislature intended. Distinctions between a 'rogue employee' scenario and directors’ involvement were acknowledged, but the core test remains knowledge of the s21(1) facts. The decision referenced the drafting history and related FSMA/1986 FSA drafting, noting interpretive consistency with Scandex and the general intention behind 'knowingly' in regulatory contexts.
